title: Immunometabolic regulation of macrophage function in cardio-hepatic-renal comorbidities: Mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities.
abstract: This review examines metabolic comorbidities affecting the heart, liver and kidney. The clinical prevalence of cardiohepatorenal metabolic comorbidities associated with obesity and type 2 diabetes is substantial. Chronic low-grade inflammation serves as the fundamental pathogenic mechanism. Abnormal macrophage activation is associated with metabolic disorders and damage to multiple organs. The conventional M1/M2 binary classification fails to adequately capture the heterogeneity of macrophages in vivo. Previous studies have primarily focused on the investigation of individual organs, leaving the cross-organ immune-metabolic linkage mechanism poorly understood. Furthermore, targeted interventions often lack precision. In this study, we systematically summarize the roles of macrophage polarization, phenotypic remodeling and metabolic activation in the injury of three metabolic organs. We also analyze their mediating functions in inter-organ immune-metabolic crosstalk and the associated pathological connections. Glycolipid toxicity impairs the glycolipid metabolism of macrophages via the NLRP3/SIRT pathway, resulting in a pro-inflammatory polarization advantage. Specific subsets of macrophages, including CCR2+,TREM2+,and CD206+CD68+,are involved in mediating myocardial remodeling, liver fibrosis, and renal interstitial injury, respectively.Medications such as SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists may provide multi-organ protection by modulating macrophage activity. The current research presents several limitations, including species differences between humans and mice, ambiguous temporal transformation rules of macrophages, and inadequate specificity of targeted preparations.Future efforts should leverage spatial multi-omics and gene editing technologies to analyze the global regulatory network and develop highly selective targeted strategies. This approach can offer theoretical support for the integrated and precise prevention and management of metabolic comorbidities.

title: Diabetes Pharmacotherapy: A Medicinal Chemistry Perspective on Conventional, Emerging, and Plant-derived Antidiabetic Agents.
abstract: Diabetes mellitus is a chronic metabolic disorder characterized by persistent hyperglycemia, arising from defective insulin secretion, impaired insulin action, or both. It represents a rapidly growing global health crisis, currently affecting over 537 million adults worldwide, with devastating microvascular and macrovascular complications including nephropathy, retinopathy, neuropathy, and cardiovascular disease risk. Current pharmacotherapy encompasses diverse drug classes targeting distinct pathophysiological mechanisms. Sulfonylureas and meglitinides stimulate insulin secretion, whereas biguanides suppress hepatic gluconeogenesis and activate AMPK. The thiazolidinediones enhance peripheral insulin sensitivity via PPAR-γ activation. The DPP-4 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists potentiate the incretin axis, whereas the SGLT-2 inhibitors promote renal glucose excretion. Amylin analogues modulate postprandial glucagon secretion. Beyond glycemic control, significant cardiovascular outcome trials, including EMPA-REG OUTCOME, DAPA-HF, DELIVER, and EMPEROR-Reduced, have established that certain agents confer significant cardio-renal protective benefits independent of their glucose-lowering effects. This review additionally surveys emerging antidiabetic compounds under clinical evaluation, including dual and triple incretin receptor agonists. The medicinal chemistry and key synthetic pathways of representative antidiabetic drugs are discussed to bridge pharmacology with chemical design, highlighting structure-activity relationships. Plant-derived antidiabetic agents are critically evaluated with emphasis laid on clinical evidence, bioavailability limitations, and regulatory considerations. A systematic literature search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and ClinicalTrials.gov, prioritizing publications from 2019 to 2025. Future directions, including AI-assisted drug discovery, pharmacogenomics, and β-cell regeneration strategies, are also discussed.

title: Direct cardiac or systemic? Reexamining the cardiovascular mechanisms of SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists.
journal: Journal of basic and clinical physiology and pharmacology
abstract: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) improve cardiovascular (CV) outcomes in type 2 diabetes mellitus, and several agents benefit patients without diabetes, yet their mechanisms remain incompletely understood. This narrative review examines whether these benefits arise from direct cardiac actions, systemic hemodynamic and metabolic effects, or both. We performed a structured PubMed search for CV outcome trials, mediation analyses, human mechanistic and imaging studies, and preclinical studies, classifying each proposed mechanism by its supporting evidence. Outcome trials consistently show that SGLT2 inhibitors reduce heart failure (HF) hospitalization and slow kidney disease progression, whereas GLP-1 RAs reduce atherosclerotic events, but these trials cannot identify the responsible mechanisms. Human data support contributions from natriuresis, decongestion, and renal hemodynamics for SGLT2 inhibitors and from glycemic, vascular, and anti-inflammatory effects for GLP-1 RAs, although mediation analyses explain only part of either class's benefit. Direct myocardial actions remain largely hypothetical in humans. The CV effects of both classes are best viewed as overlapping, interacting hemodynamic, renal, metabolic, vascular, and neurohormonal mechanisms rather than a direct-versus-systemic dichotomy. Clinically, the evidence supports prioritizing SGLT2 inhibitors for HF and chronic kidney disease and GLP-1 RAs for atherosclerotic CV disease and obesity-related risk.

title: Tirzepatide for the treatment of obstructive sleep apnea: from apnea-hypopnea index reduction to cardiometabolic risk mitigation-a narrative review.
abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a chronic respiratory disorder with nocturnal oxygen desaturation that is often associated with multisystemic sequelae such as hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, and increased morbidity and mortality. Obesity has been proposed as a modifiable risk factor; hence, the recent shift in focus to investigating anti-obesity medications for the management of OSA. Tirzepatide is the first U.S. FDA-approved pharmacotherapy for the treatment of moderate-to-severe OSA in adults with obesity to be utilized in combination with low caloric intake and physical activity, given its prior success in managing type 2 diabetes (T2D) and obesity. This narrative review evaluates tirzepatide and the SURMOUNT-OSA trial program as the key contemporary anchors for the pharmacological treatment of OSA in adults with concurrent obesity. Because the randomized evidence base currently comprises a single pivotal trial program, the review centers on SURMOUNT-OSA and its prespecified endpoints along with post hoc analyses, supplemented by observational, modeling, and mechanistic studies. In the SURMOUNT-OSA program, tirzepatide produced randomized, placebo-controlled reductions in the apnea-hypopnea index, sleep apnea-specific hypoxic burden, body weight, and systemic inflammation. The program was designed around respiratory and metabolic endpoints rather than clinical events, so it cannot support conclusions about mortality, cardiovascular, or renal outcomes. Favorable signals for those events, including all-cause mortality, major adverse kidney events, and major adverse cardiovascular events, come only from nonrandomized observational cohorts and are best regarded as directional and exploratory rather than definitive. Tirzepatide may help frame OSA as a multifactorial and partially metabolically treatable disease and may represent a clinically meaningful expansion of treatment options alongside, rather than as a replacement for, established mechanical and procedural therapies. The available evidence is anchored in a single phase 3 trial program and limited by short follow-up and the absence of definitive comparative and long-term outcome data. Long-term durability of effect after discontinuation, generalizability beyond the SURMOUNT-OSA-eligible population, OSA-specific economic analysis, and head-to-head comparisons against CPAP remain the principal unsettled questions requiring dedicated long-term studies before firm clinical recommendations can be made.

title: Diabesity: an old term, a modern challenge - multi-omics and precision anti-obesity pharmacotherapy in type 2 diabetes.
journal: Journal of pharmacy & pharmaceutical sciences : a publication of the Canadian Society for Pharmaceutical Sciences, Societe canadienne des sciences pharmaceutiques
abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and obesity are closely interconnected but heterogeneous conditions in which treatment response, safety, body weight, glycemic control, and long-term clinical outcomes vary substantially between individuals. This narrative review evaluates emerging anti-obesity pharmacotherapy in patients with coexisting T2DM and obesity and examines the translational role of multi-omics in future precision treatment selection. Distinct from reviews focused primarily on obesity pharmacotherapy or omics-based disease stratification, the present review emphasizes the interface between contemporary drug mechanisms, T2DM-associated metabolic heterogeneity, candidate molecular signatures, and the level of evidence required for clinically actionable prescribing. We summarize evidence for approved and investigational oral incretin therapies, dual and triple receptor agonists, amylin-based strategies, established antidiabetic drugs, and adjunctive approaches targeting body composition. Throughout the review, we distinguish established clinical evidence from mechanistic rationale, candidate biomarkers, exploratory associations, and hypothetical future precision applications. We also separate metabolic efficacy endpoints, such as body weight and HbA1c, from intermediate cardiometabolic risk markers and from cardiovascular or kidney outcomes demonstrated in dedicated outcome trials. At present, no genomic, metabolomic, lipidomic, proteomic, microbiome, or integrated multi-omics signature has been clinically validated to select a specific anti-obesity medication for patients with T2DM and obesity. Major unresolved issues include the need for prospective biomarker validation, direct comparative trials, standardized assays, externally validated and calibrated prediction models, preservation of skeletal muscle health and physical function, long-term safety, treatment durability, affordability, and equitable implementation. Multi-omics should therefore be viewed as an investigational framework for generating and testing precision-treatment hypotheses rather than as a basis for routine prescribing.

title: Availability of age-stratified evidence for GLP1 receptor agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors: an analysis of European public assessment reports with a focus on older patients.
abstract: GLP1 receptor agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors are widely prescribed and their use is increasingly frequent in older patient populations. We evaluated the extent to which older patients were represented in clinical trials of liraglutide, dulaglutide, semaglutide, tirzepatide, dapagliflozin and empagliflozin. To identify relevant trials, we screened the respective European Public Assessment Reports (n = 28) and the European Summaries of Product Characteristics (n = 9) for each of the six approved medicines. Further information was retrieved from the original publications of the identified trials and from the ClinicalTrials.gov database (n = 40). Overall, we analyzed n = 185 sources for 106 trial populations. For 46% of the 106 analyzed trial populations, data for patients ≥65 years were identified. Where age distributions were reported, patients aged 75 years or older were markedly underrepresented in nearly all trials, and subgroup analyses of efficacy and safety by age were rarely published. Especially in cardiovascular outcome trials and trials including patients with chronic kidney disease or chronic heart failure, older patients were better represented and analyses of primary outcomes in different age groups were published more frequently. Safety data on different age groups were mainly identified in the European Public Assessment Reports. Whereas increasing numbers of adverse events with older age were observed in several trials, this increase typically affected all trial arms, independent of the drug treatment. Data availability for patients with older age is insufficient from pivotal trials to properly describe efficacy or safety of liraglutide, dulaglutide, semaglutide, tirzepatide, dapagliflozin, or empagliflozin.

title: Complication Prevention Beyond Glycaemic Control in Type 2 Diabetes: Cumulative Metabolic Exposure, Organ Vulnerability and Treatment Durability.
abstract: Type 2 diabetes is a progressive multisystem disorder in which long-term complication burden reflects more than contemporaneous glycaemic control. Age at onset, previous metabolic exposure, obesity-related risk, organ injury, treatment safety and the capacity to sustain effective care interact across the disease course. This critical narrative review synthesised targeted PubMed/MEDLINE searches, international guidance, landmark and contemporary randomised trials, longitudinal cohorts, validated risk models and clinically influential reviews. A targeted update search was completed through 22 September 2026. The evidence supports a clinically ordered approach in which immediate treatment-related hazards are considered first, followed by established organ disease or a dominant preventable outcome, residual modifiable cardiometabolic exposure, treatment durability and the care systems required to translate evidence into sustained benefit. Historical trials established the importance of glycaemic, blood-pressure and lipid management and coordinated multifactorial intervention. Contemporary SGLT2 inhibitor and incretin-based trials add direct cardiovascular, heart-failure and kidney outcome evidence in defined populations, while MASH trials provide emerging histological evidence. HbA1c, validated risk equations and organ-specific pathways retain their established roles. The proposed framework is interpretive rather than predictive. It does not assign numerical weights or treatment thresholds but aims to identify the preventable outcome that should take priority, the intervention supported by the most relevant evidence and whether that intervention can be implemented safely and durably.

title: Bleeding and Thromboembolic Outcomes Following GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Initiation in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes and Atrial Fibrillation Receiving Direct Oral Anticoagulants: A Target Trial Emulation.
abstract: Patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) and Type 2 diabetes (T2D) require coordinated stroke prevention and metabolic risk management. Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are standard for stroke prevention, while glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) are increasingly used in T2D. In DOAC users, GLP-1RA initiation may alter body weight and gastrointestinal physiology, potentially increasing DOAC exposure and thereby elevating bleeding risk. We aim to investigate the impact of GLP-1RA initiation on risks of thromboembolic disease and bleeding in patients with T2D and AF receiving DOACs. We emulated a target trial comparing GLP-1RA versus dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitor initiation. We identified Medicare beneficiaries aged ≥ 65 years with T2D and AF receiving DOACs. Randomization was emulated using 1:1 propensity score matching. Primary outcomes include thromboembolic disease and bleeding. Per-protocol effects were estimated using inverse-probability-censoring-weighted Cox proportional hazards models. After matching, 930 patients were included in each group, with mean follow-up of 1 year. Mean age was 74.7 vs. 74.2 years, and 47.1% vs. 44.2% were women in the GLP-1RA vs. DPP-4 inhibitor groups. GLP-1RA initiation was associated with higher bleeding risk (HR 1.18, 95% CI: 1.03-1.36), lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.58, 95% CI: 0.36-0.95), and similar thromboembolic risk (HR 1.50, 95% CI: 0.22-10.43). Among DOAC-treated patients with T2D and AF, GLP-1RA initiation was associated with a less favourable bleeding profile but no evident increase in thromboembolic risk. These findings support careful clinical monitoring and further studies incorporating body weight and renal function to inform individualized treatment.

title: Changes in Metabolic and Blood Pressure Outcomes With Semaglutide Across Chronic Kidney Disease Stages: A Post Hoc Analysis of the FLOW Trial.
abstract: To assess changes in glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c), body weight, and systolic/diastolic blood pressure (SBP/DBP) by chronic kidney disease (CKD) and albuminuria categories in a post hoc analysis of FLOW, an international, double-blind, randomized, phase 3b clinical trial of adults with CKD and Type 2 diabetes (T2D). We evaluated the effect of semaglutide 1.0 mg versus placebo (in addition to standard of care) on changes in HbA1c, body weight, SBP, and DBP from baseline to Week 104 stratified by baseline estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR; ≥ 60, ≥ 45 to < 60, ≥ 30 to < 45, < 30 mL/min/1.73 m2) and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR; < 30, 30 to < 300, and ≥ 300 mg/g). Outcomes were analysed using analysis of covariance with baseline eGFR/UACR as covariates and an interaction term for treatment group by eGFR/UACR categories. We calculated the estimated treatment difference (ETD) between the semaglutide and placebo groups. FLOW included 3533 participants. Compared with participants assigned placebo, those assigned semaglutide had greater reductions in HbA1c (ETD range across eGFR/UACR groups: -0.7% to -1.0%; all p < 0.0001) and body weight (ETD: -2.5 kg to -4.6 kg; all p < 0.0001 except UACR < 30) from baseline to Week 104. Participants with lower baseline eGFR/higher UACR categories treated with semaglutide also had greater improvements in SBP than those receiving placebo. In interaction analyses, the treatment effect did not differ significantly by baseline eGFR/UACR for any of the outcomes. Semaglutide improves glycaemic control and weight, regardless of baseline eGFR or UACR, and SBP in lower eGFR/higher UACR categories.

title: Mechanistic Insights into GLP-1 and DPP-4 Pathways: Opportunities for Nano-Delivery and β-Cell Protection and Regeneration.
abstract: Diabetes mellitus is characterized by persistent hyperglycemia and progressive β-cell dysfunction. GLP-1 receptor agonists improve glycemic control and weight management, with cardiovascular and renal benefits reported in some patients, while DPP-4 inhibitors generally have more modest effects. Limitations such as peptide instability, administration challenges, tolerability, cost, and long-term treatment burden have encouraged the development of advanced drug-delivery and regenerative strategies. This narrative review evaluates the molecular mechanisms of GLP-1 and DPP-4 signaling and the therapeutic potential of emerging approaches for diabetes management. The literature was reviewed with particular emphasis on nanotechnology-based drug-delivery systems, geneand mRNA-based therapies, and cell-based strategies for incretin therapy, β-cell preservation, and regeneration. Evidence regarding therapeutic efficacy, delivery-system characteristics, development status, advantages and limitations, and barriers to clinical translation was critically examined to provide an integrated overview of current advances and future opportunities. GLP-1 signaling and DPP-4 inhibition improve glucose-dependent insulin secretion while supporting β-cell survival and function. Nanotechnology-based delivery systems show potential to improve peptide stability, bioavailability, controlled release, and tissue targeting, although most approaches remain at the preclinical stage. Gene, mRNA, and cell-based approaches have shown β-cell regeneration or preservation in animal models; however, clinically meaningful endogenous β-cell regeneration has not yet been established in humans. Key barriers to clinical translation include long-term biosafety, immunogenicity, manufacturing scalability and reproducibility, regulatory requirements, cost, and clinical implementation. Combining cutting-edge delivery technologies with well-established incretin pharmacology may help overcome some of the drawbacks of conventional treatments. However, nano-delivery, gene, mRNA, and regeneration techniques are still in preclinical or early research stages; they should be clearly distinguished from clinically proven treatments. To determine their longterm efficacy, safety, and clinical value, more validation in well-organized clinical trials is needed.. GLP-1 receptor agonists and DPP-4 inhibitors remain established components of incretin- based therapy, while advanced nanotechnology-based delivery systems offer promising opportunities but are largely supported by preclinical evidence. Future research should highlight the combination of precision medicine, pharmacogenomics, artificial intelligence-assisted treatment, and optimized drug-delivery systems to improve therapeutic efficacy and patient-specific outcomes. Smart glucose-responsive nanocarriers may further allow controlled, targeted, and adaptive drug release, supporting the development of more precise incretin-based therapies.

title: Real-World Comparison of Cardiorenal Outcomes With SGLT-2 Inhibitors Versus GLP-1 Receptor Agonists in Type 2 Diabetes.
abstract: To compare cardiorenal outcomes, mortality and safety between sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT-2i) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA) in adults with Type 2 diabetes (T2D). We conducted a retrospective, new-user cohort study using the TriNetX global federated health research network. We identified 249 237 propensity score-matched pairs (498 474 total patients) who initiated SGLT-2i or GLP-1 RA between 2018 and 2023. The primary outcome was a kidney failure/death composite, defined as kidney failure, dialysis, kidney transplantation or all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included composite cardiovascular events, mortality and safety profiles. SGLT-2i initiation was associated with a lower risk of the kidney failure/death composite compared with GLP-1 RA (HR: 0.87, 95% CI: 0.85-0.89). For the kidney-specific component, SGLT-2i initiation was associated with a lower risk of kidney failure, dialysis or kidney transplantation (HR: 0.74, 95% CI: 0.71-0.78), while all-cause mortality was also lower (HR: 0.90, 95% CI: 0.88-0.93). The composite cardiovascular outcome (myocardial infarction, stroke, acute heart failure, cardiogenic shock, cardiac arrest or death) was broadly comparable between groups (HR: 0.98, 95% CI: 0.97-1.00). SGLT-2i initiation was associated with lower risks of kidney failure-related outcomes and all-cause mortality compared with GLP-1 RA initiation, while cardiovascular outcomes were broadly comparable. These findings may inform individualized treatment selection in adults with T2D.

title: Tirzepatide-associated severe euvolemic hyponatremia with syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion-compatible biochemical features.
abstract: Tirzepatide is a dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist that is being increasingly used for the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity. Gastrointestinal adverse effects associated with incretin-based therapies can influence water balance through nonosmotic vasopressin release and reduced oral solute intake. In this case report, we report a patient who developed severe symptomatic hyponatremia with biochemical features compatible with the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion temporally associated with tirzepatide therapy. A woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus and morbid obesity on regular insulin and chronic torsemide therapy presented with anorexia, weakness, and drowsiness 10 days after tirzepatide administration. Serum sodium was 104 mmol/L, and she was clinically euvolemic. Renal, hepatic, hematologic, acid-base, and other endocrine parameters were normal. The calculated serum osmolality was 224 mOsm/kg. Urinary sodium remained elevated after withdrawal of the diuretic. The patient was managed with fluid restriction and hypertonic saline, and this resulted in progressive correction of sodium and clinical improvement. This case suggests a potential association between tirzepatide therapy and severe euvolemic hyponatremia. Clinicians should consider electrolyte monitoring in patients receiving incretin-based therapy who develop significant gastrointestinal symptoms or reduced oral intake.

title: PET Imaging of Dual GLP-1R and GIPR Targeting with [18F]AlF-NOTA-Asp2-Tirzepatide.
abstract: Tirzepatide is a clinical dual GLP-1R and GIPR agonist for type 2 diabetes and obesity, and non-invasive approaches to assess its in vivo biodistribution and systemic toxicity in living animals remain limited. Both receptors also serve as potential targets for neuroendocrine tumor imaging, and dual-target PET probes for simultaneous GLP-1R and GIPR detection are still lacking. Herein, we developed a novel PET probe [18F]AlF-NOTA-Asp2-tirzepatide via structural modification of tirzepatide. This probe successfully visualized the in vivo distribution of tirzepatide, which was primarily eliminated through the renal system. The C20 fatty diacid moiety caused elevated uptake in the heart, liver and blood due to enhanced albumin binding. In vitro assays verified its reliable GLP-1R and moderate GIPR binding affinity. Persistent tumor accumulation was observed in INS-1 and A549-GIPR xenografts, allowing effective tumor visualization. In summary, [18F]AlF-NOTA-Asp2-tirzepatide features facile radiolabeling and enables the clear visualization of tirzepatide in vivo, along with favorable dual-targeting performance, while excessive non-target uptake still needs to be optimized for further clinical translation.

title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists Versus Empagliflozin or Dapagliflozin in the MASLD-Heart Failure Phenotype: An Exploratory Propensity-Matched Cohort Study.
abstract: Treatment selection may confound observational comparisons of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) in adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and heart failure (HF). To compare recorded outcomes between treatment groups and examine whether the associations persisted after restricting the analysis by agent and diabetes status and separating early and later outcome windows. Retrospective, initiation-based, active-comparator cohort study (new-user design not verified). We used the TriNetX US Collaborative Network and a common index eligibility period from January 1, 2018, through June 2, 2026. The revised analyses were performed on September 12, 2026. An additional sensitivity analysis of acute HF excluded patients with this outcome before the start of the day 1-1825 window. The primary analysis compared semaglutide, liraglutide, or dulaglutide with empagliflozin or dapagliflozin using 1:1 propensity score matching and assessed outcomes during days 1-1825. Separate analyses of the broader GLP-1 RA group examined outcomes during days 1-90 and 91-1825 and among patients with type 2 diabetes and no recorded type 1 diabetes. We report endpoint-specific event proportions, risk differences, hazard ratios (HRs), 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and proportionality test results. The primary analysis included 8,550 patients per group after matching. Mortality occurred in 599/8,514 (7.0%) versus 861/8,509 (10.1%); the HR was 0.607 (95% CI, 0.546-0.673). Coded acute HF diagnoses occurred in 1,217/8,550 (14.2%) versus 2,525/8,550 (29.5%); the HR was 0.398 (95% CI, 0.372-0.427), with evidence of non-proportional hazards. In separately matched descriptive interval analyses (8,489 patients per group), the HR for coded acute HF was 0.262 (95% CI, 0.236-0.291) during days 1-90 and 0.507 (95% CI, 0.469-0.548) during days 91-1825. The HR for acute kidney injury during the later interval was 0.740 (95% CI, 0.650-0.842). Among 5,709 matched pairs with type 2 diabetes and no recorded type 1 diabetes, the HR for coded acute HF was 0.431 (95% CI, 0.397-0.468), whereas the HR for ketoacidosis was 0.683 (95% CI, 0.455-1.025). No advantage was observed for acute pancreatitis in any analysis. In a separate analysis excluding patients with prior acute HF, the HR was 0.421 (95% CI, 0.362-0.489), with evidence of non-proportional hazards. Albumin and bilirubin remained imbalanced in a direction favoring the GLP-1 RA group; body mass index also remained imbalanced. GLP-1 RA exposure was associated with lower observed hazards for several outcomes, and the association with coded acute HF was weaker after day 90. The early concentration and magnitude of this association make treatment channeling a plausible explanation, although this analysis cannot establish that explanation. These exploratory findings do not support causal inferences or treatment-preference conclusions and do not challenge randomized evidence supporting SGLT2i use in HF.

title: Semaglutide and Cardiovascular Death: a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Cardioprotective Efficacy of Semaglutide.
abstract: Cardiovascular death (CVD) remains a leading cause of global mortality. Although semaglutide reduces major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), the consistency and exact magnitude of its standalone effect on CVD across various patient phenotypes require comprehensive evaluation. This meta-analysis systematically evaluated the clinical efficacy of semaglutide on CVD risk across randomized controlled trials (RCTs). PubMed, Embase, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched up to July 2026 to identify RCTs comparing semaglutide with placebo in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), overweight or obesity, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) or chronic kidney disease, reporting CVD as a primary, secondary or exploratory outcome. Pooled hazard ratio (HR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated using a random-effects restricted maximum likelihood (REML) model. Publication bias and study robustness were assessed via Egger's test, Begg's test, and trim-and-fill analysis. Seven high-quality RCTs comprising 38412 patients were included. Semaglutide significantly reduced the risk of CVD by 17% compared with placebo (pooled HR = 0.83, 95% CI: 0.72-0.95; P = 0.01). Inter-study heterogeneity was low-to-moderate (I 2= 27.44%, P = 0.18). Subgroup analyses confirmed uniform benefits across different clinical phenotypes (T2DM; overweight or obesity without diabetes; and obesity-related HFpEF, with or without T2DM; P = 0.63) and administration routes (oral versus subcutaneous; P = 0.74). Meta-regression identified trial duration as a key moderator (R 2 = 85.27%, P = 0.089), whereas sex, age, BMI, HbA1c and concomitant SGLT2i therapy did not modify the treatment effect. Publication bias tests were non-significant, and trim-and-fill simulations confirmed the stability of the primary pooled estimate. Semaglutide delivers a robust and consistent 17% reduction in CVD across diverse cardiometabolic populations, including patients with T2DM, overweight or obesity without diabetes, and obesity-related HFpEF. These findings strongly support its role as a foundational cardioprotective intervention, independent of baseline glycemic status or the administration route.

title: Beyond glycemic control: cardiovascular and kidney benefits of GLP-1 receptor agonists and the dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist tirzepatide: a narrative review.
abstract: Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome reflects the complex interplay among cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, type 2 diabetes, and obesity. GLP-1 receptor agonists and tirzepatide have emerged as important therapeutic options within CKM syndrome, although the strength and maturity of evidence differ across individual agents and cardiovascular and kidney outcomes. This narrative review summarizes current evidence on the cardiovascular and kidney effects of GLP-1 receptor agonists and the dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist tirzepatide. Large randomized controlled trials have established reductions in major adverse cardiovascular events with several GLP-1 receptor agonists, while dedicated evidence for clinically meaningful chronic kidney disease progression is currently strongest for semaglutide. Cardiovascular benefits of semaglutide have also been demonstrated in individuals with overweight or obesity without type 2 diabetes, supporting effects beyond glucose lowering. Tirzepatide provides substantial improvements in glycemic control and body weight, with expanding evidence supporting cardiovascular benefit, including particularly encouraging findings in obesity-related heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. In contrast, its kidney evidence remains less mature and is derived predominantly from secondary and post-hoc analyses rather than from a dedicated kidney outcome trial. Collectively, these findings support a phenotype-oriented and multimodal role for incretin-based therapies in CKM syndrome management while highlighting important differences in the maturity of outcome evidence.

title: Pregnancy and perinatal outcomes following exposure to GLP-1 and dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists: a time-window-stratified systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: To evaluate maternal, fetal, and neonatal outcomes after preconception or gestational exposure to glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and dual glucagon-like peptide-1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide receptor agonists, and to assess the reproducibility of reported safety signals. Six databases plus a drug-level safety search were searched through 16 July 2026. Exposure was classified into four clinically defined time windows. Independent studies or data sources were the analytic unit; one primary comparator was selected per study, and odds ratios and risk ratios were synthesized separately. Random-effects meta-analysis, timing-stratified and dominant-study sensitivity analyses, Newcastle-Ottawa Scale assessment, and GRADE certainty assessment were used. Fourteen comparative data sources were included; 13 were quantitatively eligible and eight contributed to at least one pooled estimate. In the timing-specific analysis of major congenital malformations, four studies with verified periconceptional/first-trimester exposure yielded an odds ratio of 0.99 (95% confidence interval 0.77-1.27). A secondary pregnancy-period analysis that added one unadjusted, trimester-unspecified cohort yielded 1.00 (0.94-1.06); that cohort contributed 93.5% of the weight. Pooled preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth, and stillbirth analyses showed no statistically significant differences. Preeclampsia and other sparse outcomes were not pooled. Certainty was very low for all key outcomes. Current evidence does not demonstrate a clear or consistent increase in major congenital malformation risk, but very low certainty, imprecision, residual confounding, heterogeneous comparators, sparse agent-specific data, and uncertain exposure timing preclude conclusions of safety. Reported preeclampsia and renal or urinary signals have not been independently replicated.

title: Urological manifestations in obesity.
journal: Current opinion in endocrinology, diabetes, and obesity
abstract: The global prevalence of obesity continues to rise, with effects ranging across urology. This review summarizes recent evidence on obesity and its impact on various urological conditions, including malignancy, infections, stone disease, functional urology and male reproductive health, chronic kidney disease, and pediatric urology, to guide comprehensive management in this population. Obesity has a paradoxical survival benefit in patients with renal cell carcinoma, while its impact drives aggressive prostate cancer. Obesity increases kidney stone risk, with sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists showing divergent effects on lithogenesis and urinary tract infections. It is a modifiable risk factor for overactive bladder and stress urinary incontinence, both of which improve with weight loss/ bariatric surgery. Robotic surgery mitigates obesity-related perioperative risk. Hypogonadism secondary to obesity is a major reversible cause of male infertility. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA) reverse metabolic hypogonadism and helps in slowing chronic kidney progression. Maternal and childhood obesity may impair testicular descent and can also increase the risk of nocturnal enuresis. Obesity's urological effects are heterogeneous, paradoxical from pediatric to adults, mediated by insulin resistance, chronic inflammation, and hormonal dysregulation. Weight loss and the use of GLP-1 RA may offer a unique strategy for optimizing and treating urological conditions.

title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists Decrease the Rate of Rupture, Cardiac Events, and Death in Patients with Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms.
abstract: Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a degenerative condition involving several processes including inflammation, matrix remodeling, disruptions of vascular smooth muscle cells, and thrombus formation all leading to progressive dilatation of the aorta and eventual rupture. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA) are now considered part of the frontline therapeutic options to treat type 2 diabetes mellitus and have also been validated as having compelling anti-inflammatory and cardiovascular protective properties. Data is limited on the impact of GLP-1RA on outcomes of patients with AAA. The aim of this study is to examine the association and possible impact of GLP-1RA on patients with AAA. Data was sourced from the TriNetX research network, encompassing 123 health care organizations. Utilizing ICD-10 and CPT codes, we identified patients with AAA who received abdominal imaging every six months. Group 1 was comprised of patients who were treated with GLP-1RA while Group 2 patients were not. Propensity-score-matching (PSM) was used in a 1:1 fashion using age, sex, diabetes, metformin use, hypertension, cardiac disease, tobacco use, chronic kidney disease, and pulmonary disease as covariates. Primary outcomes were aneurysm rupture or repair. Secondary outcomes include mortality and major adverse cardiac events (MACE; myocardial infarction, stroke, and heart failure). Standard statistical methods were used as appropriate. We identified 412,490 patients with diagnosis of AAA who were undergoing 6-month surveillance between June 1, 2010 and April 16, 2024. After PSM, the GLP-1RA group (N=13,722) underwent fewer elective repairs at each timepoint (1.5% vs 2.3% at 2 years, 2.1% vs 3.0% at 5 years, P<.01) and had significantly fewer ruptures at two years (1.1% vs 1.8%, P<.01) and five years (1.6% vs 2.4%, P<.01) when compared to Group 2 (N=13,722). Group 1 also experienced significantly fewer MACE and all-cause mortality at two and five years. On multivariate analysis, GLP-1RA significantly reduced the risk of undergoing elective repair (HR 0.757, 95% CI [0.636-0.902], P<.01), rupture (HR 0.538, 95% CI [0.418-0.691], P<.01), all-cause mortality (HR 0.474, 95% CI [0.439-0.511], P<.001), and MACE (HR 0.825, 95% CI [0.794-0.857], P<.01) at 5 years. The use of GLP-1RA in patients with AAA is associated with fewer ruptures, elective repairs, and improved rates of MACE and death. A prospective analysis may further elucidate if GLP-1RA should be prescribed to reduce the rate of aneurysm growth.

title: Comparative adverse-event reporting patterns of semaglutide and tirzepatide: a disproportionality analysis of FAERS.
abstract: Semaglutide and tirzepatide are widely used for type 2 diabetes and obesity, but comparative post-marketing safety data remain limited. To compare adverse-event reporting patterns for semaglutide and tirzepatide in the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS), focusing on gastrointestinal, renal and ocular events, alopecia, serious outcomes, mortality, and reporting chronology. This retrospective pharmacovigilance study analyzed FAERS reports submitted from January 2022 through June 2026. After deduplication, 215,337 unique reports remained; predefined exposure criteria identified 60,423 semaglutide-only reports, 143,126 tirzepatide-only reports, and 853 reports listing both drugs without additional suspect active ingredients. Disproportionality was assessed using reporting odds ratios (RORs) with 95% confidence intervals. Multivariable logistic regression, false discovery rate adjustment, and reporting-latency analyses were also performed. Semaglutide showed higher reporting odds than tirzepatide for impaired gastric emptying (ROR 6.39), intestinal obstruction/ileus (ROR 4.56), acute kidney injury (ROR 2.51), pancreatitis (ROR 2.18), vomiting (ROR 2.11), and optic ischaemic neuropathy (ROR 15.77). Alopecia was relatively more frequently reported with tirzepatide (ROR 0.74). Semaglutide reports had higher adjusted reporting odds of hospitalization (aOR 2.80) and death (aOR 1.21). In an exploratory analysis restricted to male reports, erectile dysfunction was reported in 92 of 16,673 semaglutide reports and 46 of 27,321 tirzepatide reports (ROR 3.29, 95% CI 2.31-4.69; q < 0.001). Semaglutide and tirzepatide exhibited distinct post-marketing reporting patterns. The erectile-dysfunction finding was exploratory and hypothesis-generating. All findings reflect spontaneous reporting rather than comparative clinical risk or causality and require confirmation in population-based studies.

title: The Crossroads Between the Kidney and Gastrointestinal Disorders: Core Curriculum 2026.
journal: American journal of kidney diseases : the official journal of the National Kidney Foundation
abstract: The kidney and gastrointestinal (GI) tract are closely linked through a bidirectional system involving complex interactions called the gut-kidney axis. Within this system, alterations in the gut microbiome can promote progression of chronic kidney disease (CKD) while uremic toxins from advanced kidney dysfunction can adversely affect intestinal health. Incretin hormones, particularly glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1), play an important role in this gut-kidney signaling and will be explored here. We also examine how this physiology helps explain the connection between GI illness and IgA nephropathy, along with the kidney manifestations seen in inflammatory bowel disease. Furthermore, we will review how CKD and end-stage kidney disease increase the risk of GI disease and complicate its management, and how CKD therapies affect GI symptoms. In this AJKD Core Curriculum, we use a case-based format to illustrate the intricate interplay between the kidneys and the GI tract.

title: Obesity Medications in Older Adults: A Geriatrics 5Ms Framework for Safe and Patient-Centered Prescribing.
journal: Journal of the American Geriatrics Society
abstract: Obesity medications that act through gut-derived hormonal pathways include glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1), dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide/glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1/GIP), and emerging triple glucagon-like peptide-1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide/glucagon receptor agonists. These therapies are increasingly prescribed for weight management and glycemic control, as well as for their cardiometabolic and renal benefits. While these medications offer substantial benefits to patients across multiple health conditions, their use in older adults warrants heightened scrutiny. Older adults face increased risks of sarcopenia and frailty, and evidence from major clinical trials suggests that a substantial proportion of medication-associated weight loss agents may result in loss of lean mass, potentially posing risks for this population. Other adverse effects that may be more consequential in older adults include dehydration, malnutrition, perioperative aspiration, and fat-predominant weight regain after discontinuation. This paper provides a clinically oriented framework to guide prescribing decisions for older adults. Drawing on patient scenarios from common geriatric contexts, including frailty, cognitive impairment, glucocorticoid use, and surgical planning, we propose prescribing approaches that optimize therapeutic benefits while mitigating potential harms. We integrate these recommendations within the Geriatrics 5Ms Framework (Mind, Mobility, Medications, Multicomplexity, and Matters Most) to contextualize treatment within geriatrics practice. Lifestyle co-interventions, particularly resistance training, adequate protein intake, and ongoing functional monitoring, emerge as essential components for older adults receiving these therapies. We also discuss identifying priority areas for future research, including age-stratified clinical trials and the routine inclusion of body composition and physical function outcomes.

title: From receptor architecture to outcome maturity: a clinical framework for multiorgan incretin therapy.
journal: Endocrine practice : official journal of the American College of Endocrinology and the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists
abstract: To propose a clinically usable framework that separates receptor architecture and metabolic potency from the maturity of patient-relevant outcome evidence for incretin-based therapies. This Commentary draws on recent cardiovascular, kidney, heart failure, peripheral artery disease, liver, and emerging polyagonist evidence to define outcome maturity across five domains: endpoint directness and clinical relevance; study design and evidentiary confidence; comparator and population context; follow-up duration, durability, and safety; and molecule-, dose-, and indication-specific applicability. Four qualitative states of outcome evidence are proposed: preliminary, emerging, established, and mature. These categories apply to a specific molecule, dose, indication, phenotype, and outcome question and are intentionally nonnumeric. Outcome maturity does not measure treatment-effect magnitude or comparative drug efficacy. A six-step clinical workflow links the dominant organ-risk phenotype, clinically meaningful outcome, evidence maturity, applicability, treatment sustainability, and proportionate clinical positioning. Receptor architecture defines biological potential, whereas outcome maturity characterizes the directness, robustness, durability, and applicability of clinical evidence. Clinical positioning should remain proportional to phenotype-specific evidence and should not convert differences between nonaligned trials into cross-trial efficacy rankings.

title: Multisystem Outcomes of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists Versus Active Comparators in Type 2 Diabetes: A Multicenter Target Trial Emulation.
journal: Journal of diabetes science and technology
abstract: Multisystem effects of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) beyond cardiometabolic outcomes are incompletely characterized against active comparators in type 2 diabetes (T2D). We compared GLP-1RA with sulfonylureas (SUs), sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2is), and dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors (DPP4is) in adults with T2D. In a multicenter target trial emulation across 5 University of California academic medical centers (2012-2025) using harmonized electronic health record data, adults with T2D newly initiating GLP-1RA, SU, SGLT2i, or DPP4i were propensity score-matched 1-to-1 within site via least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (>11 000 covariates), with up to 5-year follow-up. We screened 181 prespecified incident outcomes across 15 body systems, pooling hazard ratios by random-effects meta-analysis. Robustness required leave-one-medical-center-out stability, E-value ≥1.5, and false discovery rate-adjusted P < .10. Among 70 982 matched adults, 118 robust associations were identified (65 for reduced risk and 53 for increased risk). Risk reductions were most consistent for cardiovascular outcomes, including myocarditis/cardiomyopathy (summary hazard ratio, 0.38 [95% CI, 0.32-0.44] vs SGLT2i), acute myocardial infarction (0.53 [0.42-0.66]), heart failure (0.71 [0.58-0.88] vs DPP4i), and thromboembolism (0.69-0.72), and for nephritis/nephrosis (0.73 [0.67-0.79]), nutritional anemia (0.70-0.81), coagulation disorders (0.73-0.81), and tobacco-related disorders (0.60 [0.49-0.74]). Risk increases were found for musculoskeletal conditions (22 associations); osteoarthritis 1.48 (1.29-1.68), stress fractures 1.68 (1.15-2.47), diverticular disease (1.18-1.33), sleep-wake disorders (1.27-1.54), and menopausal disorders (1.32-1.52). Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist initiation was associated with reduced cardiovascular, renal, hematologic, and tobacco-related risk, consistent with outcome trials. Increased risks for musculoskeletal, gastrointestinal, and sleep-wake disorders warrant monitoring as the clinical use of GLP-1RAs continues to expand.

title: The NLRP3 Inflammasome Across the AKI-AKD-CKD Continuum: Mitochondrial, Epigenetic and Endocrine-Metabolic Regulation.
abstract: The NLRP3 inflammasome has emerged as a potential molecular link between cellular stress, sterile inflammation, and progressive kidney damage. This review critically examines canonical, non-canonical, and mitochondrial mechanisms of NLRP3 regulation across the acute kidney injury (AKI)-acute kidney disease (AKD)-chronic kidney disease (CKD) continuum, integrating their relationships with pyroptosis, maladaptive repair, fibrosis, and epigenetic regulation. Particular attention is given to endocrine-metabolic signals that may shape renal inflammasome activity. Hyperglycemia, advanced glycation end products, mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, TXNIP signaling, lipotoxicity, impaired tubular fatty-acid oxidation, podocyte insulin resistance, obesity-related adipokine imbalance, and aldosterone-mineralocorticoid receptor activation may converge on NLRP3. Conversely, inflammasome-dependent cytokine release and pyroptosis may amplify insulin resistance, metabolic dysfunction, and cardiorenal injury, establishing a bidirectional endocrine-renal inflammatory loop. Importantly, increased NLRP3 mRNA or protein abundance is distinguished from functional inflammasome activation, which is more strongly supported by downstream evidence such as ASC recruitment/oligomerization, caspase-1 activation, mature IL-1β/IL-18 production, GSDMD cleavage, or pyroptotic cell death. A central issue is whether NLRP3 is a causal driver of kidney disease or a marker of ongoing tissue injury. Although genetic and pharmacological studies support a pathogenic role in experimental models, clinical evidence remains largely associative and disease-dependent. NLRP3-related signals should therefore be regarded as candidate, rather than validated, biomarkers. SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists and finerenone may indirectly attenuate NLRP3 signaling, but mechanistic mediation of their clinical benefits remains unproven. Defining cell-specific activation and clinical target engagement will be essential to establish NLRP3 as a biomarker and therapeutic target.

title: Obesity and Atrial Fibrillation: Weighing the Evidence.
abstract: Obesity is a major, modifiable risk factor for atrial fibrillation (AF). Potential mechanisms include haemodynamic and metabolic changes, inflammation, changes in epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) composition and cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome. EAT is increasingly recognised as a dynamic, pro-arrhythmic fat depot with a possible bidirectional relationship with AF, whereby AF itself may modulate EAT independent of weight change. CKM syndrome also underlies the complex interplay between obesity and AF. Despite guideline recommendations for at least 10% weight reduction in obese patients with AF, recent randomised trials focusing on weight reduction have largely failed to demonstrate clinically meaningful improvements in AF outcomes compared with catheter ablation or usual care. Incretin-based therapies including glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) are a promising therapy offering sustained weight loss alongside broader cardiometabolic benefits, although randomised trials with AF as a primary endpoint are lacking. Comprehensive multidisciplinary lifestyle risk factor modification (LRFM) clinics that address cardiometabolic risk factors, AF education and medication adherence have shown benefit beyond weight reduction alone, although their delivery has been heterogeneous. This narrative review examines the evolving relationship between obesity and AF including a multidimensional cardiometabolic lens, EAT characterisation, contemporary randomised trials of weight reduction, and the emerging role of incretin-based therapies and LRFM clinics.

title: Urinary Stone Recurrence After Initiation of GLP-1-Based Therapy: A Romanian Retrospective Cohort Study of Clinical, Renal, and Hydration-Related Factors.
abstract: Background: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists produce substantial weight loss and improve glycemic control, but their relationship with urinary stone recurrence remains incompletely characterized. We evaluated clinically and radiologically confirmed recurrent stone episodes occurring after initiation of semaglutide or tirzepatide. Methods: This retrospective single-center cohort screened 168 adults receiving semaglutide or tirzepatide. Four patients with previous bariatric surgery, 33 without at least 6 months of post-initiation clinical follow-up, and five with hyperparathyroidism were excluded, leaving 126 participants. Follow-up was calculated from GLP-1-based therapy initiation to the last documented clinical or imaging assessment. Recurrence required a stone episode documented before treatment initiation and a new symptomatic or radiologically progressive stone event after initiation. Results: The cohort included 94 semaglutide and 32 tirzepatide users. Median follow-up was 9 months [IQR 8-12]. Thirteen patients (10.3%; 95% CI 6.1-16.9%) had a recurrent episode after treatment initiation. No measured demographic, metabolic, renal, hydration-related, electrolyte, or treatment characteristic clearly differentiated patients with and without recurrence. Allopurinol use was more frequent among recurrent stone formers in an unadjusted analysis, a finding considered exploratory and likely affected by confounding by indication. Conclusions: In this single-arm cohort, 10.3% of patients had clinically and radiologically documented stone recurrence after GLP-1-based therapy initiation. The study describes post-initiation events but cannot estimate treatment-attributable risk because it lacked an untreated comparator, pre-treatment incidence-rate analysis, standardized surveillance, and complete exposure data. Larger prospective comparator studies with baseline imaging, time-to-event follow-up, complete urinary chemistry, and treatment-dose data are required.

title: Target Trial of Semaglutide Versus Dulaglutide or Liraglutide in Patients Receiving Hemodialysis.
abstract: To evaluate the comparative effectiveness of semaglutide versus dulaglutide or liraglutide in patients with diabetes receiving maintenance hemodialysis. Using 2011-2022 U.S. Renal Data System and Medicare data, we emulated a target trial evaluating semaglutide versus dulaglutide or liraglutide in patients receiving hemodialysis. Overlap weights were used to adjust for confounders. Fine-Gray models were used to assess death on dialysis and hospitalization. A generalized estimating equation was used for repeated measures of body weight. We identified 1,312 semaglutide and 2,601 dulaglutide or liraglutide users. After overlap weighting, the effective sample size was 3,200 patients (mean age 61; 63% White; 28% Black; 52% male; median [interquartile range] BMI 34 [29-40] kg/m2; median follow-up 1.1 [0.6-1.9] years). Semaglutide versus dulaglutide or liraglutide was associated with a mortality on dialysis subdistribution hazard ratio (sHR) of 0.82 (95% CI 0.70-0.97; 1-year cumulative incidence 11% vs. 13%) and all-cause hospitalization sHR of 0.91 (95% CI 0.83-0.99; 1-year incidence 57% vs. 62%). Body weight loss was higher with semaglutide (-4.8%, 95% CI -5.3% to -4.2%) at 1 year vs. -3.4%, 95% CI -3.9% to -3.1%). Direct comparisons of semaglutide versus dulaglutide showed similar results for mortality (sHR 0.82, 95% CI 0.69-0.97) and hospitalization (sHR 0.88, 95% CI 0.81-0.97), but semaglutide versus liraglutide showed no statistically significant benefit for mortality or hospitalization. Among patients with diabetes receiving hemodialysis and equipoise between semaglutide and dulaglutide or liraglutide, semaglutide may be the preferred glucagon-like peptide 1 agent compared with dulaglutide.

title: Diabetic Retinopathy Risk in SGLT2i vs GLP1RA Initiators With CKD Stages 3-4 and Type 2 Diabetes.
abstract: Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP1RA) have demonstrated renal and cardiovascular benefits among patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and type 2 diabetes (T2D). However, their comparative effects on diabetic retinopathy (DR) outcomes in patients with CKD stages 3-4 and T2D remain unclear. This study aimed to demonstrate the effect of SGLT2i vs GLP1RA in this population. Population-based, new-user, active comparator cohort study comparing SGLT2i versus GLP1RA initiators. Subjects were divided into 2 cohorts: (1) incident nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR) and (2) DR progression cohort. Patients with CKD stages 3-4 and T2D across 3 US health care databases: Optum's de-identified Clinformatics Data Mart Database (2014-2024), Merative MarketScan (2014-2022), and Medicare Fee-for-Service (2014-2020). Adults with a new prescription for either SGLT2i or GLP1RA without prior use in the preceding 365 days. The primary outcomes were incident NPDR and DR progression, identified through ICD-9/10 diagnosis codes and procedural codes for retinopathy treatments. Exposures, covariates, and outcomes were obtained from structured claims fields. Both cohorts were analyzed using propensity score matching (1:1) to control for confounding. Incidence rates (IRs), rate differences, and hazard ratios (HRs) were calculated. After 1:1 propensity score matching, the study included 20,135 matched patient pairs in the incident NPDR cohort and 7,763 matched pairs in the DR progression cohort. For incident NPDR, there was no difference between SGLT2i and GLP1RA groups (IR 29.55 vs 30.38 per 1,000 person-years, respectively; HR 0.98 [95% CI, 0.87-1.10]). Similarly, DR progression was not different between groups (IR 32.73 vs 35.24 per 1,000 person-years; HR 0.92 [95% CI, 0.76-1.12]). Subgroup analyses showed no differences in HRs for both incident NPDR and DR progression across multiple predefined subgroups. Potential for residual confounding, outcome misclassification, and limited generalizability to non-U.S. populations. Initiation of SGLT2i was not associated with a different risk of incident NPDR or DR progression compared with GLP1RA among patients with CKD stages 3-4 and T2D. Additional studies with extended follow-up are needed to better characterize long-term retinal safety profiles of these therapies.

title: Oral Health-Related Adverse Events of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists.
abstract: As the clinical use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) continues to grow for the management of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular and renal protection, noncirrhotic fatty liver disease, and weight management, their potential implications for oral health need to be considered. This study examined oral health-related adverse events (AEs) associated with GLP-1 RAs using postmarketing data from the US Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS). FAERS reports for available GLP-1 RAs, exenatide, liraglutide, semaglutide, dulaglutide, and tirzepatide, were screened from their initial market introduction through December 2025, identifying 364,274 total AE reports, of which 31,195 (8.6%) involved oral, craniofacial, or dental manifestations. Tirzepatide, despite being one of the most recently approved GLP-1 RAs, accounted for the highest overall AE volume, and semaglutide demonstrated the largest proportion of oral health-related AEs. A disproportionality analysis revealed a significant drug-specific signal for dry mouth of semaglutide, while vomiting, regurgitation, and reflux-related events produced a significant signal across all 5 drugs. Sensory disorders, including dysgeusia and taste disturbances, also demonstrated significant proportional reporting ratios (PRRs) and reporting odds ratios (RORs) for several GLP-1 RAs. Association analysis of AEs showed significant associations between vomiting and taste disturbances, as well as between dry mouth and dysgeusia, particularly with semaglutide and dulaglutide. This analysis highlights emerging safety signals in oral health and underscores the need for heightened clinical awareness and prospective studies to characterize the incidence, timing, and mechanisms of oral AEs associated with GLP-1 RA therapy.Knowledge Transfer Statement:Understanding the oral adverse effects associated with GLP-1 receptor agonists allows clinicians and dental providers to more effectively counsel patients initiating or continuing these medications. By recognizing early symptoms such as dry mouth, dysgeusia, and reflux-related irritation, providers can implement targeted preventive strategies-including hydration guidance, salivary substitutes, dietary modifications, and closer oral health monitoring-to reduce complications and improve patient comfort, adherence, and overall treatment outcomes. This knowledge enhances interdisciplinary management of individuals using GLP-1 RAs.

title: GLP-1 receptor agonists and adverse outcomes in patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic viral hepatitis.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA) are a novel class of anti-diabetic drugs that can treat obesity and type 2 diabetes (T2D). T2D and chronic viral hepatitis (CVH) frequently coexist and worsen liver and non-liver outcomes, but effective pharmacological therapies are limited. We aimed to evaluate the effect of GLP-1RA on liver and non-liver complications among patients with T2D and CVH in the United States. Patients with T2D and CVH initiating GLP-1RA were included (2013-2022) in Merative™ Marketscan® Research Databases. Primary outcomes included (1) hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and cirrhosis, and (2) cardiovascular disease (CVD), chronic kidney disease (CKD), and non-liver cancer. Cox proportional hazards models were conducted to estimate hazard ratio (HR) and 95% confidence interval (CI). A total of 9,499 patients with T2D and CVH were included after 1:4 propensity score matching. Compared with non-GLP-1RA (N=7,366), GLP-1RA use (N=2,133) was associated with significantly lower risks of any liver-related outcomes (HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.57-0.87; P=0.001), HCC (HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.31-0.93; P=0.028), cirrhosis (HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.56-0.86; P<0.001), CKD (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.53-0.84; P<0.001). A trend toward a lower risk of CVD (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.66-1.03; P=0.089) and non-liver cancer (HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.53-1.01; P=0.055) was observed among GLP-1RA users, although the association did not reach statistical significance. GLP-1RA use was associated with lower risks of cirrhosis, HCC, and CKD among patients with T2D and CVH, with nonsignificant trends toward lower risks of CVD and non-liver cancer.

title: Use of SGLT2 Inhibitors, GLP-1 Receptor Agonists, and DPP-4 Inhibitors in Incident Hyponatremia in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes: Multicenter Target Trial Emulations.
abstract: Hyponatremia poses risks in type 2 diabetes, yet comparative electrolyte safety across glucose-lowering therapies remains unclear. We evaluated the risk of incident hyponatremia associated with sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), and dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors in real-world practice. Using electronic health records from 155 healthcare organizations in the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network, we conducted multicenter active-comparator, new-user target trial emulations with 1:1 propensity score matching. For each pairwise comparison, adults with type 2 diabetes initiating either drug class, with no record of either class during the preceding 365 days, were included. The primary outcome was incident hyponatremia (ICD-10-CM E87.1 or serum sodium ≤ 135 mmol/L); sensitivity outcomes included diagnosis-only, laboratory-only, and stricter laboratory thresholds. Among more than 300,000 matched pairs per comparison, SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 RAs were each associated with a 15% lower hazard of hyponatremia than DPP-4 inhibitors (hazard ratio [HR], 0.850; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.842-0.858 and HR, 0.847; 95% CI: 0.838-0.856). The lower risk persisted at stricter sodium thresholds and across clinically relevant subgroups, including patients with heart failure, chronic kidney disease, or high-risk medications use. SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 RAs were broadly comparable (HR, 0.962; 95% CI: 0.952-0.971). Positive and negative control outcomes were consistent with expectations. Overall, SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 RAs were associated with a lower risk of incident hyponatremia than DPP-4 inhibitors. These real-world findings provide reassurance regarding the electrolyte safety of SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 RAs, complementing their established cardiorenal benefits.

title: Skeletal Muscle in Vulnerable Populations Receiving Cardiorenal-Metabolic Therapies: SGLT2 Inhibitors, Incretin-Based Therapies, and the Challenge of Precision Medicine.
abstract: The introduction of sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors and incretin-based therapies has transformed the management of obesity, type 2 diabetes, heart failure, and chronic kidney disease by delivering substantial metabolic, cardiovascular, and renal benefits. However, their effects on skeletal muscle have become a growing area of interest. While SGLT2 inhibitors induce modest weight loss, their catabolic metabolic effects have prompted questions regarding skeletal muscle preservation, particularly in individuals with limited physiological reserve. Conversely, the profound weight loss achieved with incretin-based therapies has raised concerns about accompanying reductions in lean tissue and their potential functional consequences. In this narrative review, we critically evaluate the available evidence regarding the effects of these therapeutic classes on skeletal muscle, integrating findings from randomized controlled trials, observational studies, systematic reviews, and mechanistic investigations. We compare their distinct biological mechanisms; summarize clinical evidence on changes in muscle quantity, quality, strength, and physical performance; and discuss their implications for older adults; individuals with frailty, sarcopenia, or sarcopenic obesity; and patients with heart failure or chronic kidney disease. Overall, current evidence indicates that both SGLT2 inhibitors and incretin-based therapies preferentially reduce adipose tissue, whereas the accompanying reductions in lean tissue are generally proportional to the magnitude of weight loss. Importantly, reductions in lean tissue should not be equated with treatment-induced sarcopenia, as current evidence does not consistently demonstrate clinically meaningful impairment in muscle strength or physical performance. Nevertheless, the populations most susceptible to skeletal muscle dysfunction remain underrepresented in clinical trials. We discuss a phenotype-based approach that integrates skeletal muscle health into therapeutic decision-making and outline practical strategies-including resistance exercise, adequate protein intake, and individualized monitoring-to preserve muscle function during treatment. Future research should prioritize standardized functional outcomes and dedicated studies in vulnerable populations to enable precision cardiorenal-metabolic medicine.

title: Real-World Pharmacological Patterns and Residual Cardiometabolic Risk in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes in Romania.
abstract: Contemporary management of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) has shifted from a glucose-centered approach toward integrated cardio-renal-metabolic protection. Although sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), and intensive lipid-lowering therapies have demonstrated substantial cardiovascular and renal benefits, implementation in routine outpatient care and the burden of persistent residual risk remain insufficiently characterized in Romania. We aimed to evaluate routine-care pharmacological treatment patterns, identify residual cardio-renal-metabolic risk despite ongoing therapy, determine independent correlates of persistent adverse outcomes, and explore potential therapeutic gaps in adults with T2DM. This cross-sectional observational study included 232 unique adults with T2DM attending a specialized outpatient diabetes clinic in Romania between 1 October 2024 and 19 February 2026. One eligible outpatient record per participant was analyzed; when multiple records were available, the earliest eligible record in the exported dataset was used as the index visit. No a priori sample-size calculation was performed. Pharmacological therapies, cardiovascular and renal phenotypes, metabolic biomarkers, and clinical outcomes were extracted from routinely collected electronic medical records. Residual risk was evaluated using glycemic, lipid, renal, obesity, and blood-pressure targets. Multivariable logistic regression analyses identified independent correlates of persistent cardio-metabolic abnormalities. An exploratory cumulative residual-risk count was constructed by summing seven clinically relevant uncontrolled risk factors. Biguanides were the most frequently prescribed glucose-lowering agents (53.0%), followed by SGLT2 inhibitors (44.8%), insulin (32.3% of the total cohort), GLP-1 receptor agonists (15.5%), and DPP-4 inhibitors (14.7%). Statins were prescribed to 48.7% of participants. SGLT2 inhibitor use did not differ significantly according to established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease phenotypes, whereas GLP-1 receptor agonists were prescribed more frequently in participants with obesity (22.0% vs. 7.6%, p = 0.003). Clinically important residual risk persisted across all treatment groups. Among SGLT2 inhibitor users, 57.3% had HbA1c ≥ 7%, while 27.9% remained albuminuric. Among insulin-treated participants, 84.0% had HbA1c ≥ 7%; reduced eGFR and albuminuria were also more frequent than among non-users. Despite statin therapy, 33.6% of treated participants continued to exhibit LDL cholesterol ≥ 100 mg/dL. In multivariable logistic regression, insulin therapy was associated with higher odds of HbA1c ≥ 7% (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 7.41, 95% confidence interval [CI] 3.50-15.65), while SGLT2 inhibitor therapy was associated with lower odds of albuminuria (aOR 0.54, 95% CI 0.30-0.95). Absence of statin-containing therapy was associated with higher odds of LDL cholesterol ≥ 100 mg/dL (aOR 6.01, 95% CI 3.38-10.66). Absence of statin-containing therapy was associated with higher odds of residual LDL cholesterol ≥ 100 mg/dL (aOR 4.21, 95% CI 2.34-7.58). Seventy-two percent of participants presented at least three persistent cardio-renal-metabolic abnormalities, while 24.2% exhibited five or more. More than half of participants with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease were not receiving either an SGLT2 inhibitor or a GLP-1 receptor agonist. Significant residual cardio-renal-metabolic risk persists in adults with T2DM despite use of contemporary pharmacological therapies. Disease severity markers and treatment exposure were associated with persistent adverse outcomes, but the cross-sectional design does not establish causality. The study identified potentially modifiable therapeutic gaps among patients with established cardiovascular and renal disease. Comprehensive and repeatedly reassessed cardio-renal-metabolic management, integrating pharmacological optimization with individualized risk stratification, may improve implementation of guideline-directed therapy and reduce long-term complications in routine clinical practice.

title: GLP-1-based therapies in cardiovascular disease: outcomes, mechanisms, and emerging clinical applications.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) have shown cardiovascular benefits beyond their established role in treating type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). This review evaluates recent clinical evidence, potential mechanisms, and the expanding use of GLP-1-based therapies in cardiovascular disease. We reviewed major randomized clinical trials assessing cardiovascular, kidney, and heart failure outcomes, along with related mechanistic studies and clinical guidelines published through July 2026. Early trials, including LEADER, SUSTAIN-6, and REWIND, reported 12%-26% reductions in major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in patients with T2DM. More recent trials have extended these findings to other populations. SELECT showed a 20% reduction in MACE among individuals with obesity and established cardiovascular disease but without diabetes, while FLOW demonstrated a 24% reduction in its primary kidney composite outcome. SOUL reported a 14% reduction in MACE with oral semaglutide, and SUMMIT showed a 38% reduction in cardiovascular death or worsening heart failure with tirzepatide. SURPASS-CVOT found tirzepatide to be noninferior, but not superior, to dulaglutide for MACE. These benefits likely involve several mechanisms beyond glucose lowering and weight loss, although gastrointestinal adverse effects still remain a concern. Growing clinical evidence supports the use of GLP-1-based therapies beyond diabetes management, particularly in patients with cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, or obesity-related heart failure. Further studies will be needed to understand their mechanisms better, long-term safety, and optimal use in clinical practice.

title: Modern antidiabetic therapy in older adults with type 2 diabetes: evidence, best practice and a clinical pharmacist's framework.
abstract: Older adults with type 2 diabetes require treatment that balances cardiovascular and kidney protection against hypoglycemia, treatment burden, undernutrition, and functional vulnerability. This narrative review considers PubMed-indexed literature and ClinicalTrials.gov records covering January 2010-October 2026, with targeted updating on 12 October 2026. It examines sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, tirzepatide, and dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors. Age-stratified outcome evidence is distinguished from whole-trial results and the limited evidence in adults aged 80 years or older. Body-composition findings, neurodegenerative outcomes, kidney-protective treatment, and pharmacist-supported regimen modification are critically appraised. Organ protection and glycemic simplification should be considered separately. Frailty is not synonymous with kidney impairment, and reductions in lean mass do not establish treatment-induced sarcopenia. Weight-neutral therapy remains useful when weight loss is undesirable. A structured medication review should integrate patient priorities, nutrition, physical performance, renal function, and hypoglycemia risk, followed by explicit monitoring and communication across care transitions. Prospective validation of this integrated framework in the oldest and most vulnerable populations is needed.

title: The Veterans Affairs Pentoxifylline in Diabetic Kidney Disease (VA PTXRx) Study: Baseline Characteristics.
journal: Nephrology, dialysis, transplantation : official publication of the European Dialysis and Transplant Association - European Renal Association
abstract: Experimental and clinical data suggest that the non-specific phosphodiesterase inhibitor pentoxifylline (PTX) reduces proteinuria and may delay the progression of diabetic kidney disease (DKD). However, no large-scale randomized clinical trial has determined whether PTX can reduce end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) and mortality in DKD. VA PTXRx is a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, multicenter clinical trial designed to test the hypothesis that PTX, when added to usual care, prolongs the time to kidney failure or death in type 2 diabetic (T2D) participants with DKD compared to usual care plus placebo. Enrolled participants at very high risk for ESKD and/or death were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to either PTX 400 mg twice daily or matching placebo using randomly permuted blocks with stratification for site, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone (RAAS) inhibitor use, and chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage. The study is event-driven, requiring 646 primary events (ESKD (chronic dialysis or transplantation) or death) to achieve 80% power to detect a relative risk reduction of 19% with PTX. Between December 2019 and November 2025, 2376 participants at 34 VA sites in the USA were randomized. The mean age at randomization was 72.3 years (SD 7.7), with 97% being male. The mean baseline eGFR was 33.3 mL/min/1.73 m2 (SD 9.4). The median urinary albumin to creatinine ratio (UACR) was 401 mg/g (IQR 122-1076). At baseline, the usage of RAAS inhibitors was 80.0%, sodium-glucose transporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors 52.9%, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists 33.2%, and finerenone 3.0%. The majority (88%) of participants had stage 3B or 4 CKD (eGFR < 45 mL/min/1.73m2). The results, anticipated in 2027, are expected to determine whether PTX is a treatment option for patients with high-risk DKD. Because PTX is a generic medication, it is inexpensive in many health systems, which would facilitate access if it proves effective. Trial Registration: This study is registered with clinicaltrials.gov (Identifier: NCT03625648).

title: Lessons from dog lifespan therapeutics for their human companions.
abstract: The growing evidence that existing cardio-renal-metabolic therapies, such as GLP-1 receptor agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors, confer all-cause mortality benefits has positioned them as the first wave of potential gerotherapeutics. However, repurposing these drugs for a lifespan extension indication remains constrained by trial duration, misaligned incentives, and the lack of a viable regulatory path.
